body.text: The Serbian student movement’s success in the October 25 election has coincided with the young protesters in India attempting to turn their campaign into lasting political change. Despite obvious differences between the two nations, the Serbian experience carries some parallels for India.

A campaign becomes politically consequential only when it moves beyond the immediate outrage, sheds personal ego, and develops the capacity to organise society. The Serbian students took to the streets after a canopy collapsed at a railway station in November 2024, killing 16 people. But they soon consolidated their outrage into a national campaign against the government.

The Jantar Mantar campaign also began with a singular cause: the resignation of the Education Minister following a series of paper leaks that pushed several students to end their lives. Having secured the Minister’s resignation, the protesters have entered the second phase, with a long road ahead.

The Serbs could sustain the momentum because they worked without a personality-centred leadership, refused to align themselves with any political party, and followed a decentralised structure, which saw decisions emerging from collective deliberations.

People embraced their agenda because it was fresh and untested, and did not require them to subscribe to any existing political manifesto. Once the masses joined in as the rightful owners of the movement, the state found it difficult to discredit it.

In contrast, Indian student leaders tend to follow the personality cult prevailing in mainstream political parties. A handful of names acquire an importance disproportionate to their actual influence. The tendency to turn leaders into icons dilutes the campaign once the icon falls.
The Serbian experience suggests that a movement should cultivate hundreds of leaders rather than hinge on a few eminent names.

Indian youth leaders have also shown a tendency to get co-opted by political parties. Joining politics is a legitimate career move, but such accommodation often comes at the cost of the idealism that had made their activism look endearing; worse still, they suddenly become vulnerable to smear campaigns.
The case for groundwork

As the young protesters in India seek to scale up their campaign, they may also acknowledge that the Serbs took their campaign away from the power centres and turned a student protest into a wider social movement. They used social media effectively, but also launched door-to-door campaigns. They knew that the social media visibility must be supplemented by groundwork to bring about electoral change. It is easier to win an argument on X or Instagram than to initiate a meaningful conversation in society.

Like their Indian counterparts, the Serbs, too, faced hostile media. Aleksandar Vučić, who was then President, himself accused them of being foreign stooges, a charge not unknown to India. But by taking the campaign to the grassroots, the Serbian students gained acceptance beyond the immediate urban centres.

As they grew, the students broadened their programme to include institutional reform, transparency, and related issues. In retrospect, the choice to remain a pressure group also helped the Serbian students. By resisting the temptation to become a political party and maintaining an independent voice, they could translate their movement into an electoral project when the moment arrived.

Perhaps the most instructive aspect of their entire campaign was that the student assemblies chose a 250-candidate list—most drawn from outside their ranks. The youth could thereby signal that the elections were not a vehicle for igniting their own political careers. By including doctors, academics, economists, artists, farmers, bankers, even sportspersons—people who had little political experience—the students made their list representative and inclusive. It also brought home the message that the students wanted real change, not immediate gains for themselves.

Compare it with the experiment the Aam Aadmi Party had once promised. It also fielded eminent people and professionals from different fields, but the party became inseparable from its central leader, weakening the moral authority it had once enjoyed.
Beyond student politics

The Serbian experiment has shown that a successful student movement need not always produce politicians. Its achievement may lie in creating a political alternative without making its own leaders the beneficiaries of the struggle. It marks a radical departure from the trajectory of student politics in India, where campus activism serves as a launching pad for political careers. Universities are great nurseries for future politicians, but India has often witnessed energetic and infectious young voices lose their promise and independence upon submitting themselves to the bureaucracies of political parties.

In the last few decades, Indian student movements have often struggled at precisely this juncture. They succeed in mobilising people, but rarely translate the mobilisation into lasting institutional change. The Belgian historian Anton Jäger calls this phenomenon hyperpolitics, extreme politicisation without enduring political consequences.

India, clearly, is not Serbia. The two countries have vastly different political histories, electoral systems and social structures. India’s deeply entrenched inequalities and federal character rule out any direct import of the Serbian model. But the underlying principles travel fairly well: young people can build alliances without abandoning their independence, can offer a dream without possessing all the answers.

That said, the Serbs now face questions about the task of governing a country. Since the students have transferred most of the political representation to people outside their ranks, how will they ensure that the new representatives remain accountable to the movement? The newly elected MPs possess their own constitutional mandates. The students cannot simply recall them.
Perhaps the bigger question is this: now that formal power rests with the elected representatives, what course should the movement take?

The closest Indian precedents are Mahatma Gandhi and Jayaprakash Narayan. Both demonstrated that moral authority could mobilise society on a scale that conventional politics could scarcely achieve. Both also confronted the limitations of influencing political power without directly exercising it.
Gandhi died as India was moving away from the political order he had envisioned, and JP met a disillusioned end following the fate of the movement he had led.
Ashutosh Bhardwaj is an independent writer and journalist.
